title: You remember pain by its ending

lines.text: People would rather suffer longer, as long as it ends better.
In 1993, Daniel Kahneman asked people to hold a hand in cold water, at 14 degrees.
Trial two: the same 60 seconds, plus 30 more, while the water got slightly warmer.
When asked which to repeat, people were more willing to choose the longer one.
It's called the peak-end rule. We judge an experience by its most intense moment, and how it ends.
The same thing showed up in a colonoscopy study. A gentler ending made people rate it as less unpleasant.
So if you want a memory to last, make sure it ends well.

sources.claim: Kahneman et al. (1993): 60 s at 14 °C vs 60 s plus 30 s while water warmed to 15 °C; subjects more willing to repeat the longer trial
Redelmeier, Katz & Kahneman (2003): a gentler extended colonoscopy ending was rated less unpleasant

publish.title: You Remember Pain by How It Ends 🧊
publish.description: People chose 90 seconds of cold water over 60, because it ended better. The peak-end rule explains how memory really works.
publish.pinned_comment: Can you think of a bad day that was saved by a good ending? 👇
